Desktop density

The phone's 52px rows and 44px handle stay on the phone. Here an option is a 34px row: a small radio, the label, and its detail on the same line. Question tabs sit in a 36px pane header next to the accent label. Send is a 30px button.

The divider is a 10px bar, the way an editor splits panes.

Fit-to-card and the user's limit work as on the phone. On a tall screen a short question leaves the reply most of the 1,260px, and the limit stops a long one from taking it.

The split is vertical at every desktop width, so a landscape laptop gets the same stacking. The reply keeps a 760px measure either way. On the right, a 260px rail holds the visit (turns, time), the docs in play with their version and approval, the facts, and Stop agent. › collapses it to a 36px strip that keeps the counts and the stop button.

brief.md v2+12−19from v1Show changes

Leaderboard screen

One screen reached from the title menu and the end-of-game screen. It shows the top 10 scores from Game.Scores.top/1 with name, score and date.

Your row

When you are outside the top 10, your best score is pinned under a divider at the bottom. What the row shows is open.

Out of scope

A weekly tab. It needs a date on every score, which #41 doesn't store yet. Follow-up: a ticket after #41 merges.

Done when

  • the screen opens from both places
  • ties order by time set, as #41 decides
  • an empty table shows one line saying so

With width, Read opens the document beside the conversation instead of over it, so you read v2 while you talk about it. The passage behind the open question is highlighted there too. Accept drops its confirmation from the row, anchored to the button, with the same warning as the phone: the open question stays unanswered, and Answer first or Accept anyway. The details rail folds away while the document is open.

Persist the high score table

Scores live in a SQLite file under $FORGE_DATA_DIR, opened once at boot by Game.Scores.

Steps

  1. Add the schema and a migration.
  2. Write record/2 and top/1.

The release isn't a ticket type you pick, as today: only a project admin starts it, from the project page. It moves into the project's + New sheet as its own block under ticket and chat, with today's optional note. It shows only to admins. 21dThe release block · its other four states
⇡A release is open
Only one at a time. It is a ticket like any other.#46 Release 0.32 ›
⇡Can't start
The release, .forge/workflows/release.yml, cannot start: its first state names no prompt.The note you typed is kept here.
⇡No release
No workflow in the project sets release: true, so it has no release to start. Set it in the workflow file that should be the release, under .forge/workflows/.
⇡Two releases
release.yml and ship.yml both set release: true, so the project has no release; keep the flag on one.

Today's five states, in today's words. Only ready (21c) has a button. The rest say why there isn't one and what to change. A note typed before the state changed is kept, as today ("Shown, not lost").

On a tall screen everything fits in one column without views. Open tickets come first as a table. Each 52px row has the same fields as the phone's three lines: the title with the latest line under it, the step and its track, then what it is doing, usage and age. The history follows, folded to its newest four. Then proposals, merge queue and conversations as dense 36–40px rows, and the workflow last, as a map. Each step is a box with its job and budget, the steps are joined left to right, and the skip and the failed-check loop are drawn as arcs. The dots are the open tickets in each step. Proposals decide in their row. The rail is the ticket's rail with project facts, and Release opens its note in place.

◌Why is the build so slow on CI?· chat · 20m · 1 of 3Open chat ›

Cache textures by content hash

The asset step keys its cache on the commit hash, so every push rebuilds all 212 textures and the step takes six to seven minutes.

Keying each texture on a hash of its source file and its import settings rebuilds only what changed. The import settings live in assets/import.toml, so a change there invalidates every texture it covers, which is correct.

Done when
  • a push that touches no texture skips the step in under 20s
  • changing one PNG rebuilds one texture
  • the cache survives a runner restart
Out of scope

Audio and level files, which are copied, not built.

Losing the connection adds no row and no button. The top bar itself changes: a red hatched ground, a 2px red rule, and its first line becomes Not connected with a crossed-out signal. The second line counts down to the automatic retry and says when the page last heard anything, so there is nothing to press. A confirmation looks nothing like a decision. It's a round, raised pill floating over the content above the bottom bar, with an icon and two lines. It has no button and doesn't take taps (they pass through to the page), so it can vanish under a finger without harm. It never pushes anything, and it goes after four seconds. The approval row it confirms has already gone, because the decision was made.

A failure is never a toast, because it needs a response and a toast can't hold one safely. The error appears inside the dropdown you acted from, in red, in the server's words, with the next step as a button in that same panel. It stays until you close it. Errors with no panel (a failed send in a chat) show under the message they belong to.

The light theme isn't the dark one inverted. Its neutrals are cool, a faint blue-grey around hue 250, so the warm accents stand apart from the page instead of muddying it. Every accent gets a light-specific value. The amber fill is brighter and yellower, so it reads as a highlight on white. As text it turns a deep orange, as in 1 of 4 and the current step.
